title: From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs
claim: Two routes from the same inputs, internal representations and observed behavior, yield similarity matrices that can be directly correlated to measure alignment.
layout: Single panel, top-down fork into two parallel branches, double-arrow comparison at bottom
description: A top-down flow diagram. At the top, a box labeled V holds four color-coded word tiles (dog, cat, rat, fox). An arrow leads to a central 'Language Model' box, which splits into two parallel branches. The left branch is 'Hidden-State Extraction', with pseudocode h_l(w) ← encode_l(w). It leads to a 2-D plot H_l of colored vectors, then to a viridis-colored 4x4 similarity heatmap S^hid_l. The right branch is 'Behavioral Experiment', with pseudocode b_w ← behavior(w). It leads to a vector plot B, then to a heatmap S^beh. The vector colors match the word tiles. A horizontal double-headed arrow at the bottom, labeled r_l(S^hid_l, S^beh), connects the two heatmaps. The eye goes first to the top word tiles, then down both branches to the comparison.
caption: Conceptual overview. For a shared vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, we (i) extract layer-$\ell$ word representations to form a hidden-state similarity matrix $S^{\mathrm{hid}}_\ell$, and (ii) run behavioral association tasks (forced choice/free association) to build a cue--response matrix $B$ and behavioral similarity $S^{\mathrm{beh}}$. RSA correlates the pairwise similarities in $S^{\mathrm{hid}}_\ell$ and $S^{\mathrm{beh}}$ to quantify behavior--activation alignment.
abstract: We investigate the extent to which an LLM's hidden-state geometry can be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments. Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models, we run two experimental paradigms -- similarity-based forced choice and free association -- over a shared 5,000-word vocabulary, collecting 17.5M+ trials to build behavior-based similarity matrices. Using representational similarity analysis, we compare behavioral geometries to layerwise hidden-state similarity and benchmark against FastText, BERT, and cross-model consensus. We find that forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association. In a held-out-words regression, behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry. Finally, we discuss implications for the ability of behavioral tasks to uncover hidden cognitive states.
